content: Frizzled proteins belong to a family of G protein-coupled receptor proteins that function as receptors in the Wnt signaling pathway and other signaling pathways. Upon activation, Frizzled proteins initiate the activation of Dishevelled in the cytoplasm. These proteins, along with the genes encoding them, have been identified across a wide range of animal species, from sponges to humans. Frizzled proteins play critical roles in regulating cellular polarity, embryonic development, neural synapse formation, cell proliferation, and numerous other processes in both developing and mature organisms. Mutations in the human Frizzled-4 receptor have been associated with familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, a rare retinal disease that affects the retina at the back of the eye and the vitreous, the clear gel-like substance inside the eye. In Drosophila, the frizzled (fz) locus is responsible for coordinating the cytoskeletons of epidermal cells, resulting in a parallel arrangement of cuticular hairs and bristles. In fz mutants, the orientation of individual hairs is disrupted, both in relation to their neighboring cells and to the organism as a whole. In the wild-type wing, all hairs are oriented toward the distal tip. During wing development, Frizzled has two essential functions: it is required for the proximal-to-distal transmission of an intracellular polarity signal, and it is necessary for cells to respond to this polarity signal. The frizzled gene produces an mRNA that encodes an integral membrane protein with seven predicted transmembrane domains. This protein is expected to contain both extracellular and cytoplasmic domains, which are likely involved in the transmission and interpretation of polarity information.
